sections.title: Level 2 Thinking and Strategy
sections.content: In Level 2, questions are not direct. First, the given symbols must be decoded, then all statements should be connected to form a continuous chain. Usually, conclusions are derived in 3–4 steps. The Magic Box method is very useful here.

sections.title: Decoding Symbols (Magic Box Method)
sections.content: Sometimes special symbols are given instead of >, <, =. For example: @ means >, # means ≤. First write the correct meaning of all symbols. Then convert each statement into normal inequalities. Finally, connect them in one line. Do not draw conclusions without decoding.

sections.title: Connecting 3–4 Disjointed Statements
sections.content: Example: A > B, C ≥ D, B = C, D > E. First find the common variable. Since B = C, we get A > C. From C ≥ D and D > E, we get C > E. Finally, the chain becomes: A > C ≥ D > E. Now the relationship becomes clear.

sections.title: Fill in the Blanks Logic
sections.content: Question: Which symbols should be placed in A _ B _ C _ D so that A > D is definitely true? Solution: Arrange the order so that A is the largest and D is the smallest. Example: A > B ≥ C > D. Also remember that when ≥ or ≤ appears, consider both possibilities so that A > D remains true in every case.

sections.title: Definitely True vs Definitely False
sections.content: Definitely True: When the conclusion is correct in every situation. Definitely False: When the conclusion is wrong in every situation. Does Not Follow: When it may be correct sometimes and wrong sometimes. Example: A > B ≥ C. Conclusion: C > A (Definitely False). Conclusion: A > C (Definitely True).

sections.title: Complex Either/Or (3 Elements)
sections.content: If the statement is A ≥ B ≥ C and the conclusions are I: A > C, II: A = C. Both cannot be true together, but one must be true. Therefore, the answer is Either I or II. If boundaries are mutually exclusive (such as A > B and A < B), both cannot be true together.

sections.title: 4-Step Evaluation Process
sections.content: Step 1: Decode the symbols. Step 2: Build the chain using common variables. Step 3: Consider both possibilities for ≥ and ≤. Step 4: Check the conclusion in every case — only then decide True, False, or Either/Or.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Decoding symbols incorrectly. 2. Not completing the chain fully. 3. Treating ≥ only as >. 4. Confusing Definitely False with Does Not Follow.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 2, first decode, then connect, and then check all possibilities. A conclusion is definite only if the same result appears in every possible case. The Magic Box method is the key to success.

tricks.title: Magic Box Rule
tricks.explanation: First write the meaning of all symbols in a box, then solve the question.

tricks.title: Find the Strongest Direction
tricks.explanation: Identify the largest and smallest elements in the chain.
tricks.example: A > B ≥ C > D → A is largest, D is smallest

tricks.title: Break ≥ into Two Cases
tricks.example: X ≥ Y → X > Y or X = Y

tricks.title: Common Variable Linking
tricks.explanation: Connect two statements using the common letter.
tricks.example: P > Q, Q ≤ R → P > Q ≤ R

tricks.title: Fill Blank Smartly
tricks.explanation: If A > D is required, keep the order decreasing.

tricks.title: Identify Definitely False
tricks.explanation: If the conclusion is opposite to the chain, it is immediately False.
tricks.example: M > N ≥ O → O > M is wrong

tricks.title: Either/Or Boundary Trick
tricks.explanation: When two exclusive possibilities of the same relation are given.
tricks.example: A ≥ C → I. A > C II. A = C → Either I or II

tricks.title: Be Careful with Disconnected Cases
tricks.explanation: If two variables have no link, the conclusion cannot be drawn.
tricks.example: A > B, C > D → Relationship between A and C is uncertain

tricks.title: Final Chain Visualization
tricks.explanation: Write the entire chain in one line and compare the extremes.
